systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Vérification des sources complémentaires : avant de rédiger, vérifie que chaque SOURCE numérotée à partir de 2 traite bien du MÊME fait que la SOURCE 1 (même événement, mêmes acteurs). Ignore entièrement celles qui n'en traitent pas et donne leurs numéros dans « sources_ecartees ». Si, sans elles, la matière ne suffit pas pour un article fiable, réponds seulement {"insuffisant": true, "titre": "…", "texte": "…"} : une brève en français (titre de 90 caractères au plus, 2 à 3 phrases d'environ 450 caractères), uniquement d'après la SOURCE 1.
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Le texte réunit plusieurs sources sur le même sujet (SOURCE 1, SOURCE 2…). Croise-les sans rien ajouter ; si elles divergent, dis-le en nommant la source.
Source : NPR
Rubrique : États-Unis
Date du flux : 13/11/2026
Auteur : Joel Rose
Titre d'origine : What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop

ARTICLE :
SOURCE 1 (NPR) :
What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stopThe Federal Aviation Administration took an extraordinary step Friday afternoon by issuing a nationwide ground stop. No planes are taking off at any airport and millions of passengers are stranded.
The Federal Aviation Administration took an extraordinary step Friday afternoon by issuing a nationwide ground stop. No planes are taking off at any airport and millions of passengers are stranded.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews.
Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

SOURCE 2 (Al Jazeera) :
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop that halted departing flights across the United States for more than four hours after a “communication issue” affected air traffic control centres.
The FAA announced at 8:15pm Eastern time on Friday (01:15 GMT on Saturday) that it had lifted the order, after it issued the ground stop hours earlier at 3:54pm (20:54 GMT).
Airlines face delays and cancellations as they get aircraft and crews back into position.
The FAA said in a post on X in the afternoon that there had been a “temporary telecommunications outage” and that, as a precaution, all flights were being halted.
International flights would be handled case by case, it added.
More than 10,000 flights were delayed and over 4,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware, CBS News reported.
Some 4,042 flights were in the air, heading to US airports, when the ground stop was ordered, according to the tracking site Flightradar24.
The communication issue affected all 22 air route traffic control centres, which guide aircraft.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no indication that the ground stop was triggered by a threat to the US.
“Everybody’s safe. The flights are accounted for,” he said. “This is not another 9/11.”
President Donald Trump had been briefed, he added.
Asked whether a planned rollout of a new AI tool meant to help air traffic controllers could be to blame, Mullin said officials have not ruled it out. “You just can’t rule out anything at this point. We are going through that process,” he said.
The FBI does not believe a cyberattack or criminal activity caused the failure, Bloomberg reported, citing an official familiar with the matter.
The cited official said investigators were examining whether a software update could have caused the outage, though the cause had not been determined.
Democratic Senator Tammy Duckworth has called for a “thorough and complete investigation” of the reported FAA communication issues.
“The safety of our skies is built on redundancies. Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation,” Duckworth wrote in a post on X.
“As Aviation Subcommittee Ranking Member, I’ll be demanding answers from the FAA,” she added.
The disruption is the latest sign of strain on the US air traffic control system, which has been beset by equipment failures, communications problems and shortages of controllers, as the FAA tries to replace ageing infrastructure.
Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company behind the FAA’s AI-powered air traffic management system, said its technology was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.
“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a post on X.
The FAA awarded ASI an $875m contract in June to develop and deploy the SMART system, which uses artificial intelligence to support air traffic management.
The agency announced an expansion of the system across its 22 air traffic control centres on November 10, just days before the nationwide flight suspension.
US rail service affected
Amtrak, the US national rail operator, announced that its website and app are showing error messages and that customers are having difficulty reaching a representative, as it faces higher-than-normal call volumes because of the nationwide disruption to air travel.
“We apologize for the error messages on both our website and app, as well as the difficulty reaching a representative,” Amtrak said in a post on X in response to a complaint.
“We’re currently experiencing higher-than-normal call volumes due to ongoing airline issues,” the company said.
It recommended that customers try the services later.
Pilot and former FAA safety team representative Kyle Bailey told Al Jazeera: “Whether you are an expert or not, the bottom line is we’re still trying to piece the puzzle together, and it would be impossible to have an answer to the issue quickly, in a few hours at least.”
“But it is very alarming what we saw, and possibly [rail operator] Amtrak is being affected too,” he added. “The FAA’s priority at the moment is keeping not only the American passenger safe, but everyone flying in the US flight system.”
Bailey said that “halting the flights on the ground is the safest thing to do until they could figure out what’s going on. If anybody says they think they know what’s causing this problem at such an early stage, they’re not being honest”.
Congress approved $12.5bn for the overhaul last year, and the Department of Transportation and the White House asked lawmakers on Friday for another $30.1bn.
This was the first nationwide US ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last time had been after the September 11, 2001, attacks.
US authorities have yet to determine the cause of the telecommunications outage that prompted the ground stop.

SOURCE 3 (CBS News) :
A rare nationwide ground stop on all departing U.S. flights that lasted several hours Friday has been lifted, the Federal Aviation Administration said. The FAA and White House said the issue appeared to be caused by a "telecommunication outage."
"At 8:15 tonight, Eastern time, we've opened up the airspace," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said during a news briefing Friday night. "Now does that mean every flight is going to fly right now? It's going to be slow. So if you're watching, you're at an airport, check with your airline."
The FAA had issued the ground stop on all departing flights due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." The ground stop lasted about five hours.
Duffy attributed the ground stop to outdated air traffic control technology and routers overloaded by data.
"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said in the news conference. "... Our routers actually got overloaded with data and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down."
An update to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage, multiple sources told CBS News earlier Friday. The system is operated by L3Harris, which did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
Duffy said the FAA would try to move as many flights as possible Friday night depending on crew capacity.
"If not, we're going to start tomorrow [Saturday] morning with our airline partners moving those aircraft. But it's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.
There were more than 10,000 delays and over 4,000 cancellations listed Friday, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.
Duffy said he thinks flights would be "back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel" during the Thanksgiving holiday.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters in a briefing outside the White House earlier Friday that "there was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now."
"There is no indication, we had no reason to believe, that as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin said. "This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights. And all the flights are accounted for."
Mullin reiterated Friday night that there was no cyberattack and the ground stop was not related to the massive global .
"I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft," Mullin said. "I know a lot of people are making that jump. This is so far what we've seen. There is actually no cyberattack. We're still working through that process."
He also said flights will be able to land safely.
"We are assured that everybody is safe. Everybody that's going to be in the air, that's currently on the plane, the loved ones, as I said, we're going to get you on the ground and we're doing it in a safe manner," Mullin said.
Federal agencies are all working together on the situation, Mullin added.
"I don't want to say that this is a crisis, but it is because we're ... we had to do a nationwide ground stoppage," he said.
International flights departing from the East Coast can fly over the Atlantic Ocean, while flights from Jacksonville, Houston, Miami and San Juan can depart southbound over the Gulf and Atlantic, a source told CBS News.
According to the flight tracking site FlightRadar24, there were about 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports when the ground stop began. Mullin said all airborne flights were being dealt with on a "case-by-case" basis.
The ground stop was posted to the FAA's National Airspace System Status website. Delays began piling up at major airports across the country in , , , , , and .
"This is absolutely unprecedented," said Robert Sumwalt, a former chair of the National Transportation Safety Board and a CBS News transportation safety expert. "I was an airline pilot for 24 years. I was in the air on 9/11. That was the last major ground stop. There was one back in 2023 for just a few hours. This is absolutely unbelievable that this could happen in this day and age."
Duffy renewed his call in a news conference for Congress to approve emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.
"But you will have more of these," Duffy said. "You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build."
Shortly before the FAA ordered the nationwide ground stop, both major , O'Hare International and Midway International, were issued a ground stop because of an equipment outage.
In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop was ordered for a few hours, and domestic flights were due to an FAA system outage. The FAA said at the time that its flight personnel alert system went down overnight.
